messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Duc was thirty-two when a routine stomach cramp became sepsis. He remembered the ambulance ride as a blur of sirens and the paramedic’s voice saying his blood pressure was dropping. The hospital smelled of antiseptic; a doctor’s face appeared above him, then vanished. He spent six days in the ICU with a central line and a ventilator, and when he finally went home, he carried the discharge papers like a death sentence he had somehow escaped.

In the months that followed, Duc could not shake the feeling that he had come back defective. “There is something wrong with me as a person,” he told himself, and this belief soon seeped into everything. He felt hollow—dead inside—and that emotional numbness only confirmed his worst suspicion: he was weak. The weakness was the worst part, because it meant he could not trust his own body to keep him alive. As a UX designer, Duc spent his days fine‑tuning interfaces for other people’s ease, yet he could not engineer safety for himself. When a colleague said, “You look healthy now,” he smiled but felt nothing; he knew better.

The first time he drove past the hospital on his way to work, his chest tightened and his hands gripped the wheel until his knuckles went white. He began taking a different route. Soon he was avoiding any medical cue—a Red Cross van, a doctor’s office sign, even a box of surgical masks in a drugstore. His wife noticed he flinched when she mentioned her annual physical. “I just don’t want to think about it,” he said, and he meant it: he actively pushed away any memory of the ICU. The act of avoidance, however, did not calm him. Instead, it sharpened his hypervigilance. On the rare occasions he allowed himself to remember the beeping monitors, he felt a surge of anxiety that lasted for hours, leaving his body tense and ready to react. That constant alertness, in turn, reinforced his belief that he was inherently fragile—why else would his body stay on guard? The causal loop tightened: because he saw himself as weak, he avoided more; because he avoided, the world felt more dangerous; because it felt dangerous, he believed even more strongly that something was fundamentally broken in him.

Duc’s threat system locked onto anything uncertain. When a software build took longer than expected, he instantly assumed the worst—a server crash, a lost job, a cascade of failures. At stand‑up meetings, if a teammate paused before answering, his stomach dropped. “What’s wrong?” he would ask, his voice pitched high. He could not trust reassurances. “No one can convince me I’m safe,” he admitted to himself. Even after his doctors had cleared him, he felt no relief; his body stayed coiled, as if danger were always two seconds away. That physical tension exhausted him, and exhaustion fed his sense of being weak. He started avoiding situations that put his body under any stress—a brisk walk, climbing stairs, even carrying groceries—because the rise in heart rate felt too close to the panic of the ICU.

Work suffered. He stopped volunteering for projects with tight deadlines because the threat of delays was unbearable. He declined team‑building hikes, claiming he was busy. His wife grew worried. “You never come with me anymore,” she said softly. Duc wanted to explain that staying home was the only way he could keep a lid on the terror, but the words felt stuck. Emotional numbness had hollowed out even his marriage.

What finally brought him to a therapist was a single moment: his boss scheduled a quarterly review, and Duc spent three days convinced he was about to be fired. The review went fine—praise, even—but the dread did not lift. He sat in his car afterward, trembling, and realized this was not about his job. He was exhausted from living in a world where every small delay felt like the beginning of the end, and he no longer knew who he was without that fear. He wanted to trust safety again. He wanted to believe he was not weak. But mostly, he wanted the constant weight in his chest to go away.
